description: Israel had a saying about sour grapes and blaming the generation before. God tells them each person stands before Him on their own.
excerpt: As long as we're pointing at someone else for why our life is the way it is, we're stuck. Nothing can change. We've handed the keys to our own life over to somebody else.
verse: "For all people are mine to judge, both parents and children alike. And this is my rule: The person who sins is the one who will die."
body_html:
The people of Israel had a saying going around. Their parents had eaten sour grapes, and now their mouths were the ones puckering. In other words, we're just paying for what the generation before us did. None of this is our fault. God hears them repeating it and tells them to stop.

Then He lays out this rule. Each person stands before Me on their own. Parents aren't punished for their children, and children aren't punished for their parents. Every person is judged by their own choices.

We live in a time where excuses are the main thing people reach for. Nobody wants to take responsibility for anything. We'd rather blame our upbringing, our circumstances, our generation, our country, our history. Some people want reparations for things that happened hundreds of years ago to people they never met, and some want to be released from responsibility for choices they're making today because of something that happened to them when they were young.

God isn't harsh for pushing back on that. He's being kind. Because as long as we're pointing at someone else for why our life is the way it is, we're stuck. Nothing can change. We've handed the keys to our own life over to somebody else.

If we spent the same energy on our own lives that we spend blaming other people, our lives would actually look different.

You can get caught in a pattern where what you're looking for is what you find. Look for reasons to stay stuck, and you'll find them everywhere. Look for ways to take responsibility and grow, and those show up too. God is trying to break the first mindset in Ezekiel 18. He walks through three generations to make the point. A good father, a wicked son, a good grandson. Each one is judged on his own life. Not the one before him.

There were good kings and bad kings in Israel's history. Each one stood before God for himself. Your parents might have been one or the other. Your grandparents might have been one or the other. That doesn't decide who you are.

You have a choice. And you're the one who answers for it.

Where have you been using someone else's story as a reason to not take responsibility for your own?
question: Where have you been using someone else's story as a reason to not take responsibility for your own?
